Absolutely, particularly in rocket league and battlefield.

For me, a usual rocket league game is played with teammates that I have never played with before. There is also no voice communication in-game, so I communicate with my teammates in three ways, the first being the in-game chat using preset messages. The second way is through "body" language, by which I mean this: when I see a teammate move their in-game character a certain way in reaction to the current situation in-game, I can get a good idea of what they are planning to do next. The third way is knowing the unwritten rules that the community (loosely) follows. Of course, each individual player's body language and general play-style is different, so for each game I must adapt to how my teammates play. This translates generally to learning how to work with people in the real world.

It is similar for battlefield: I am usually playing with people I have never played with before. A typical game is myself and about 60 other players versus a similarly-sized second team. Teams are divided into squads of about five people. The best squads usually have at least one person filling each of four in-game roles with different specializations. I work together with my squad alongside the other squads on my team to capture and defend various objectives spread throughout the map. Ultimately, this game is won and lost by squads, not individual players. A skilled player loses to a squad of mediocre players, but a squad of skilled players cooperating is very hard to beat. Similarly, an excellent programmer reaches their full potential only as part of a team.

Yes, I believe that playing video-games has made me a better team player. The games that I play¬† require a high degree of teamwork, and more importantly have taught me to be much kinder and understanding of other's idea's and mistakes.

column14: I think my gaming does help me become a better team player because many of the games I play require communication and trust, which are key things you need in a team. One of the games I play, Hell Let Loose, is a WWII game where it's two 50ish player sides fighting against each other to take objectives. It's set up so a team has one commander, squad leaders leading infantry, armor, or recon (sniper) squads; then troopers under the squad leaders fulfilling different roles like setting down supplies, building things, or have a specific gun that only certain roles has like a rocket launcher. Each squad has their own chat channel and, besides proximity chat, the squad leaders are the only ones who can talk to other squad leaders and the commander. You could do your own thing and not talk to anyone, but that will only lead to many deaths, frustration, and a swift defeat. Therefore, it's important they you learn how to communicate with your team if you have any hope of achieving victory. Your squad can only be so big and only so many roles can be filled, so you got to talk with your team to figure out what's needed to effectively take or hold an objective or destroy a key target like a tank along with communicate where enemies are coming from so you can effectively counter them. I learned quickly that saying "They're over there" is not helpful at all. There are also points in the game where all the squads are full so you got to make your own squad. It's pretty tough because you got to communicate with other squads and the commander to make sure things are getting down while also making sure you have a handle of your squad's situation and they have everything they need to deal with it. Your squad can't see other squad's markings, so you have to learn what information you're getting is important to the squad to relay to them. It can get pretty draining, especially when you have to deal with people who don't care to take orders, but I learned that by communicating and trusting other people to do their job that not only do we win more often, but it's also a lot better and more fun time. You can also pull off some pretty impressive maneuvers with effective communication, such as making a big flank with your squad that can lead to decimating the enemy and taking the objective.¬†
